vpip.justification: Heads-up you post a blind in every hand against a single opponent, so most starting hands are worth playing and folding much more than a third of them gives your blinds away.

pfr.justification: With only one opponent the first raise often takes the pot straight away, so you should raise most hands you play from the button and a fair share from the big blind.

aggression.justification: One opponent misses the flop most of the time, so your bets and raises should clearly outnumber your calls, while some calls with strong hands let a bluffer keep betting.

wtsd.justification: Heads-up even ace-high often wins, so you should reach showdown in a large share of the flops you see, but not with every hand that misses.

wsd.justification: Heads-up you should win about half of your showdowns, since a much higher rate means you fold too often and a much lower one means you call with too little.

vpip.justification: At six players about one hand in four is strong enough to play, because the blinds come round often but several opponents still act after you.

pfr.justification: Most hands worth playing at six players are worth a raise, so your raising rate should sit only a few points below your VPIP.

aggression.justification: In fixed limit the bettor wins the pot whenever everyone folds, so after the flop a solid player bets and raises more often than they call.

wtsd.justification: At six players you should go to showdown with roughly a third of the flops you see, folding the hands that miss and cannot pay the price of a bet.

wsd.justification: A sound six-player style wins about half of its showdowns or a little more, and a much lower rate means you call down with too many weak hands.

vpip.justification: With nine or ten players someone behind you holds a strong hand more often, so only about one hand in six is worth playing.

pfr.justification: At a full table you should still raise most of the hands you play, so your raising rate stays only a few points below your VPIP.

aggression.justification: A full table does not change the value of betting first after the flop, so your bets and raises should still outnumber your calls.

wtsd.justification: At a full table you see flops with stronger hands but against more opponents, so reaching showdown with about a third of your flops is a healthy balance.

wsd.justification: Because you enter full-ring pots with stronger hands, you should win about half of the showdowns you reach or slightly more.
